\documentclass[11pt]{article}
\usepackage[margin=1in]{geometry}
\title{Do Rainfall Shocks Affect Informal Credit?
Evidence from Rural Cooperatives}
\author{A.~Diallo and P.~Srisai}
\date{June 2026}
\begin{document}
\maketitle
\begin{abstract}
We study how negative rainfall shocks reshape borrowing and lending
within rural cooperatives in the Mekong delta.\footnote{A Chinese
version of this abstract is available from the authors upon request.}
Using eleven rounds of household panel data matched with village-level
rainfall records, we show that failed monsoons increase the demand for
informal loans while simultaneously shrinking the supply of credit
inside cooperative networks.
The contraction in supply is driven by deposit withdrawals rather than
by default risk, and it persists for two growing seasons.
Cooperatives that hold buffer savings at the district level smooth
lending almost fully, suggesting a low-cost institutional fix.
\end{abstract}
\section{Introduction}
Informal credit fills the gap left by formal banking for most rural
households in the delta, and cooperative networks are its backbone.
Yet these networks pool the savings of households whose incomes move
together with the weather, which raises a natural question: what
happens to credit when a negative rainfall shock hits all members at
once?
This paper answers the question with household panel data and a new
matching of loan ledgers to village-level rainfall records.
\section{Data}
The cooperative census covers 212 village cooperatives and their loan
ledgers from 2012 to 2022.
Household interviews were conducted in eleven rounds with a rotating
panel of 3,400 households.
Rainfall records come from the national meteorological service and are
aggregated to the village growing season.
\section{Results}
A failed monsoon raises the probability that a household seeks an
informal loan by 9 percentage points.
At the same time, cooperative lending volume falls by 14 percent in
the season of the shock and remains 6 percent below trend one year
later.
Default rates barely move, while deposit withdrawals spike, which
identifies the supply channel.
\section{Conclusion}
Rainfall shocks squeeze informal credit from the supply side, not the
repayment side.
District-level buffer savings effectively insure village cooperatives
against this squeeze and deserve policy attention.
\end{document}
